name: Ramelteon
lead: Ramelteon is a prescription melatonin receptor agonist taken by mouth for insomnia characterised by difficulty falling asleep. It binds the MT1 and MT2 melatonin receptors with several times the affinity of melatonin itself and, according to its US label, has no appreciable affinity for the GABA receptor complex used by benzodiazepines and Z-drugs.[2][14] It was approved by the US FDA in July 2005 under the brand name Rozerem and is not a controlled substance in the United States.[1][14]

Its link to appearance runs through sleep and recovery: falling asleep sooner and sleeping more consistently supports recovery between training sessions, daytime energy and the rested look of skin and eyes. Its documented use is medical, and no published study has examined ramelteon for an appearance outcome.

Trials report small reductions in the time taken to fall asleep compared with placebo; a 2009 pooled analysis put the reduction at about 13 minutes on the first nights, while later meta-analyses of longer use reported subjective latency reductions of about 4 to 7 minutes.[14] The 2017 American Academy of Sleep Medicine guideline gave a weak recommendation for sleep-onset insomnia, and the European Union has not authorised ramelteon.[1][3][14]

paras: The US label indicates ramelteon for insomnia characterised by difficulty with sleep onset, with supporting trials up to six months long [2]. Reviews of the trial data describe reductions in latency to persistent sleep on the order of 10 to 19 minutes versus placebo, with smaller gains in total sleep time [1]. Phase 3 programmes enrolled adults and elderly people with chronic insomnia and healthy volunteers with transient insomnia [5][6][7].

Ramelteon has also been studied in delayed sleep phase syndrome and jet lag, and in a randomised placebo-controlled trial for prevention of delirium in hospitalised older patients [8][9][10]. Those uses are not part of the US label.

A 2009 pooled analysis found the 8 mg strength shortened sleep onset by about 13 minutes (roughly 30 percent) versus placebo over the first two nights; later meta-analyses of longer use found smaller reductions of about 4 to 7 minutes in subjective latency, and effects on total sleep time were mixed.[14] Ramelteon is not recommended in severe sleep apnoea, and the 2017 AASM guideline's recommendation rests on very low-quality evidence.[3][14]

The most common reactions listed on the label (at least 3% and more frequent than placebo) are somnolence, dizziness, fatigue, nausea and worsened insomnia [2]. Warnings cover rare angioedema and anaphylaxis, complex sleep behaviours such as sleep-driving, worsening depression, and possible effects on reproductive hormones such as prolactin and testosterone [1][2]. Co-use with fluvoxamine is contraindicated because it raises ramelteon exposure [1].

Wikipedia reports that effects such as somnolence and dizziness are only slightly more frequent than with placebo, that prolactin rises modestly in women and free testosterone falls slightly, and that the drug has low dependence liability with no known abuse potential or withdrawal.[14] Rodent studies showed liver and testicular tumours only at exposures at least 20 times the human dose.[14] Other strong CYP1A2, CYP3A4 or CYP2C9 inhibitors call for caution, and rifampin may reduce effectiveness.[14]

Ramelteon acts as an agonist at MT1 and MT2 receptors, which are thought to be involved in the circadian rhythm that underlies the sleep-wake cycle; it shows roughly an 8-fold preference for MT1 over MT2 and 3 to 16 times melatonin's affinity.[2][11][14] A 2005 neurochemical study characterised it as a selective MT1/MT2 agonist.[11]

Oral bioavailability is about 1.8 percent because of extensive first-pass metabolism, mainly by CYP1A2; peak levels occur around 45 minutes and food delays and increases absorption.[14] The active metabolite M-II circulates at 20 to 100 times the parent exposure but is much less potent, and the half-life is 1 to 2.6 hours for ramelteon versus 20 to 45 minutes for melatonin.[14] Exposure is higher in elderly adults.[14]

Ramelteon was developed by Takeda, whose programme code was TAK-375, and was approved by the FDA in July 2005 for long-term use as the first prescription drug of its melatonin-agonist class.[1][11][14] The European Medicines Agency concluded in 2008 that the benefit was not shown to outweigh risks, and it was not authorised there.[1][14]

Ramelteon is prescription-only in the US and is not a controlled substance in nearly every country; in Brazil it is listed as Class C1.[14] No looksmaxxing community discussion of ramelteon was identified; it appears in this wiki because of its sleep and circadian role.

Registered phase 3 trials of ramelteon in chronic insomnia enrolled 405 to 1,213 participants each, including an elderly-only trial of 829 participants [5][12][13]. A phase 2 trial examined delayed sleep phase syndrome and a phase 4 trial examined jet-lag insomnia [8][9]. A 2014 randomised placebo-controlled trial in JAMA Psychiatry reported less delirium with ramelteon in acutely ill older patients [10]. Guideline and network meta-analysis authors characterise its effect on sleep onset as small [3][4]. No studies were found on ramelteon for appearance outcomes. Wikipedia describes the delirium evidence as positive in a 2014 review and as suggesting benefit mainly in combination with suvorexant in a 2022 review, and the evidence for circadian rhythm disorders as mixed.[14]

card.summary: A prescription melatonin-receptor sleep drug with small, medical-only evidence and nothing on appearance.
card.note: Prescription insomnia drug; no appearance studies exist.

quick.overview:
Ramelteon is a prescription drug for trouble falling asleep. It works on the same receptors as the body's own melatonin rather than on the GABA system.

Trials show it shortens the time to fall asleep by roughly 10 to 19 minutes versus placebo. No studies have examined it for appearance outcomes.
quick.mechanism: It activates MT1 and MT2 melatonin receptors thought to be involved in the sleep-wake rhythm, and is quickly cleared from the body.
quick.risks: Labelled adverse effects include somnolence, dizziness, fatigue and nausea, with rare allergic reactions and complex sleep behaviours. It is Rx-only in the US, not a controlled substance, and not authorised in the EU.

chain: Activates MT1 and MT2 melatonin receptors
Sleep onset comes a little sooner
More consistent rest for recovery, energy and a rested look
angle.text: Ramelteon is a prescription sleep-onset drug. Better and more regular sleep is the route by which it could support recovery and a rested appearance; it has not been tested for appearance directly.
